prostate-cancer.name: Prostate cancer
prostate-cancer.definition: Prostate cancer is a cancer that starts in the prostate, a small gland in the male reproductive system that sits just below the bladder.
prostate-cancer.overview: Prostate cancer may not cause any symptoms at first. The NHS says it often grows slowly and may never cause problems, which is why monitoring is a common first step in some cases. The NHS lists being over 50, being from a Black ethnic background and having a family history of prostate cancer as factors that raise risk. The NHS says there is no national prostate cancer screening programme, and a PSA blood test is not routinely offered, although men can ask a GP about it. Treatment options include monitoring, surgery, radiotherapy and hormone therapy.

signs: An enlarged or hard-feeling prostate found on digital rectal examination
Unintended weight loss in advanced disease
complications: Spread of the cancer beyond the prostate, which may need chemotherapy
Lower back pain, tiredness and weight loss as the cancer advances
Treatment side effects such as urinary leakage and erection problems
prostate-cancer.diagnosis: The NHS says there is no single test for prostate cancer. The most commonly used are blood tests, a digital rectal examination, an MRI scan and a biopsy. If a specialist suspects cancer, an MRI scan is arranged, and a biopsy may follow to take a tissue sample to check for cancer cells. If cancer is confirmed, further scans such as CT, MRI, PET or a bone scan may help plan treatment.
prostate-cancer.treatment: The NHS describes monitoring, surgery, radiotherapy and hormone therapy as the main approaches, with chemotherapy for cancer that has spread. Active surveillance involves regular PSA tests, MRI scans and sometimes biopsies so that any progression is found early, and aims to avoid unnecessary treatment of harmless cancers. Surgery to remove the prostate and radiotherapy can both cause urinary and erection problems. Hormone therapy works by reducing the effect of testosterone on the cancer and does not cure it on its own, but can slow it down and help symptoms.
prostate-cancer.prevention: The sources retrieved do not describe a proven way to prevent prostate cancer. The NHS says men can ask a GP about a PSA blood test even without symptoms, and the GP will consider their cancer risk to help decide whether it is right for them.
prostate-cancer.seekCare: The NHS advises speaking to a GP, as a routine appointment, if you have symptoms such as problems passing urine, blood in the urine or lower back pain, or if you are worried about your risk of prostate cancer. These symptoms do not mean a person definitely has prostate cancer.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of prostate cancer?
sections.body:
The NHS says prostate cancer may not cause any symptoms at first. When symptoms do appear, they are mainly changes to passing urine. The NHS lists needing to pass urine more often, getting up in the night to pass urine, difficulty starting or keeping a steady stream, and a weak flow. Blood in the urine is also listed.

Later symptoms can include lower back pain, tiredness and weight loss without trying, which the NHS links with more advanced disease. Many of these symptoms have other causes, such as an enlarged prostate, and having them does not mean a person definitely has prostate cancer. Because early prostate cancer may cause nothing noticeable, the absence of symptoms does not rule it out.

sections.heading: Who is at higher risk of prostate cancer?
sections.body:
Macmillan describes age as the strongest risk factor, with prostate cancer uncommon under the age of 50 and more common over 75. The NHS lists being over 50, being from a Black ethnic background and having a family history of prostate cancer as factors that raise risk. Macmillan adds that Black men are also more likely to develop prostate cancer at a younger age, and that the reason is not clear but may involve genetic factors.

Macmillan says having a father or brother with prostate cancer raises a man's risk, and that the risk is greater if the relative was diagnosed under 65. BRCA2 gene variants have the clearest link among inherited gene changes, according to Macmillan. The NHS also notes that close relatives with pancreatic, breast or ovarian cancer, particularly at a young age, can be a sign that inherited genes are involved.

sections.heading: Is there a screening programme for prostate cancer?
sections.body:
The NHS says there is no national screening programme for prostate cancer. A PSA blood test is not routinely offered on the NHS, with the exception of people whose genetic tests have shown a faulty BRCA2 gene. The NHS says a man can still ask a GP for a PSA blood test even without symptoms, and the GP will consider his cancer risk to help decide whether the test is right for him.

A PSA blood test measures a protein made by the prostate. The NHS says a high result does not mean a person has cancer, because other causes such as an enlarged prostate are possible. If the level stays high, the GP may discuss referral for further tests such as a biopsy and an MRI scan.

sections.heading: How is prostate cancer diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS says there is no single test for prostate cancer. The most commonly used are blood tests, a digital rectal examination, an MRI scan and a biopsy. In a digital rectal examination, a doctor feels the prostate through the back passage.

If a specialist suspects cancer, the next step is an MRI scan. If more information is needed, a biopsy may be suggested, in which a small needle is put into the prostate to take a tissue sample to be checked for cancer cells. If cancer is confirmed, further tests such as a CT scan, MRI scan, PET scan or bone scan may be used to help plan treatment.

sections.heading: How is prostate cancer treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says prostate cancer often grows slowly and may never cause problems, so monitoring is a common first step for some people. Active surveillance involves regular PSA tests, MRI scans and sometimes biopsies, so that any sign of progression is found as early as possible. NHS 111 Wales says it aims to avoid unnecessary treatment of harmless cancers while still treating men who need it.

When treatment is needed, the main options are surgery to remove the prostate, radiotherapy and hormone therapy, and chemotherapy may be needed if the cancer has spread. Hormone therapy reduces the effect of testosterone on the cancer, and the NHS says it does not cure prostate cancer on its own but can slow it down and help with symptoms. Brachytherapy is a form of radiotherapy delivered from inside the prostate.

Treatments have side effects. Surgery and radiotherapy can both affect urine control and erections. Radiotherapy can also cause tiredness, diarrhoea and bowel irritation, and hormone therapy can cause hot flushes, tiredness, weight gain, reduced sexual desire and thinning of the bones.

sections.heading: Living with prostate cancer and the outlook
sections.body:
The NHS 111 Wales page notes that prostate cancer can come back after treatment, and that a doctor can estimate the chance of this from factors such as the PSA level and the stage of the cancer. A clinical summary of the ProtecT trial reports that deaths specifically from prostate cancer were low at a median of 10 years whatever treatment men were assigned, and that active surveillance is reasonable for some men. Active surveillance is described as regular PSA tests, MRI scans and sometimes biopsies, so that any progression is found as early as possible.

Side effects of treatment, including urinary and sexual problems, are described by the NHS as part of the picture, and a specialist team can discuss how treatment is likely to affect an individual.

faqs.q: Does the NHS screen for prostate cancer?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no national prostate cancer screening programme. A PSA blood test is not routinely offered, except for people whose genetic tests have shown a faulty BRCA2 gene. A man can ask his GP about a PSA test even without symptoms, and the GP will consider his risk.

faqs.q: Does a high PSA result mean I have prostate cancer?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says a high PSA result does not mean a person has cancer, because other causes such as an enlarged prostate are possible. If the level stays high, a GP may discuss referral for further tests such as a biopsy and an MRI scan.

faqs.q: Does prostate cancer always cause symptoms?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says prostate cancer may not cause symptoms at first. When symptoms appear they can include changes to passing urine, lower back pain, tiredness and weight loss. Many of these have other causes, so a GP can help work out what is behind them.

faqs.q: Will every prostate cancer need treatment?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. The NHS says prostate cancer often grows slowly and may never cause problems. Active surveillance, with regular PSA tests, MRI scans and sometimes biopsies, aims to avoid unnecessary treatment of harmless cancers while still treating men who need it.

faqs.q: Who is at higher risk of prostate cancer?
faqs.a: The NHS lists being over 50, being from a Black ethnic background and having a family history of prostate cancer. Macmillan describes BRCA2 gene variants as having the clearest link among inherited gene changes.

faqs.q: Who should I speak to if I am worried?
faqs.a: The NHS advises speaking to a GP if you have symptoms or are worried about your risk of prostate cancer. It is usually a routine appointment, and a GP can explain the pros and cons of testing.
